source_text: Quod licet in tanta luce consistat, ut nihil aut absolutius inveniatur aut verius, tamen pollicitus eram hoc ipsum divinae me legis testimonio comprobare, id est iniquissimum esse, si generantium scelera nascentibus eorum liberis imputentur, sicque id adversari Deum, ut etiam in sua lege praescripserit, ne tale quidquam iudicantium deformitas perpetraret. Hoc me ergo spoponderam redditurum, sed, quoniam secundus liber apostoli Pauli exponen dis est sententiis occupatus, huius voluminis primis partibus fidem congruit promissionis impleri. Legimus ergo in Deuteronomio in catalogo praeceptorum, quibus vita et conversatio populi illius ordinatur, etiam hoc apertissime a Deo fuisse mandatum; nam ut de praecedentibus et de sequentibus, inter quae sit collocatum, possit intellegi: Non fraudabis - inquit - mercedem pauperis et egentis ex fratribus tuis aut ex proselytis, qui sunt in civitatibus tuis; quotidianam reddes mercedem illius, non occidat sol super eam, quia pauper est et in ea habet spem; et non proclamabit contra te ad Dominum et erit in te peccatum. Non morientur patres pro filiis et filii non morientur pro patribus; unusquisque in suo peccato morietur [n13] .
pass_a_gloss: Although this stands in so great a light that nothing either more absolute or more true is found, nevertheless I had promised to prove this very thing by the testimony of the divine law, that is that it is most unjust if the crimes of those generating are imputed to their children being born, and that God so opposes this that he has even prescribed in his own law that the deformity of those judging should not perpetrate any such thing. This therefore I had pledged I would render; but since the second book is occupied with explaining the apostle Paul's sentences, it is fitting that the faith of the promise be fulfilled in the first parts of this volume. We read therefore in Deuteronomy, in the catalogue of precepts by which the life and conduct of that people is ordered, that this also was most openly commanded by God; for that it may be understood from the preceding and following among which it is placed: You shall not defraud, he says, the wage of the poor and needy from your brothers or from the sojourners who are in your cities; you shall render his daily wage, the sun shall not set upon it, because he is poor and has hope in it; and he shall not cry out against you to the Lord and there will be sin in you. Fathers shall not die for sons and sons shall not die for fathers; each one shall die in his own sin.

pass_b_english: Although this is so obvious that nothing could be more decisive or more true, I had promised to prove this very point by the testimony of divine law: it would be utterly unjust to charge newborn children with their parents’ crimes. God is so opposed to this that he expressly forbade judges in his law to perpetrate anything so disgraceful. I had therefore promised to establish this. But since the second book was occupied with explaining statements of the apostle Paul, it is fitting to fulfill that promise in the opening part of this book.

We read in Deuteronomy, among the commands ordering that people’s life and conduct, that God also gave this entirely explicit command. To show where it stands among the preceding and following provisions, he says: ‘You shall not withhold the wages of a poor and needy worker, whether one of your own people or one of the foreigners living in your towns. You shall pay his wages daily; the sun must not set before you pay them, because he is poor and places his hope in them. Otherwise he may cry to the Lord against you, and you will be guilty of sin. Fathers shall not die for their children, and children shall not die for their fathers. Each person shall die for his own sin’ (Deuteronomy 24:14–16).
